SIMBAD TAP, queried 2026-09-25. The source of every number in
site/src/data/galaxies.js, kept so a wrong coordinate is a test failure
rather than a wrong arrow. test/galaxies.test.mjs parses this file and
compares it to the shipped module, field by field.

Service: https://simbad.u-strasbg.fr/simbad/sim-tap/sync

Query, verbatim:

  SELECT main_id, ra, dec, V, galdim_majaxis, galdim_minaxis
  FROM basic JOIN allfluxes ON oid = oidref
  WHERE main_id IN ('NAME LMC','NAME SMC','M  31','M  33',
                    'NAME Centaurus A','M  81','M  83','M 101','NGC    55',
                    'M 104','M 110','M  32','NGC  6822','NGC   300','M  94')
  ORDER BY V ASC

Those fifteen are the brightest by V from this query, run without the name
filter and ordered by V:

  SELECT main_id, otype_txt, ra, dec, V, galdim_majaxis
  FROM basic JOIN allfluxes ON oid = oidref
  WHERE otype = 'G..' AND V IS NOT NULL AND V < 8.7 ORDER BY V ASC

with six rows left out. WHAT WAS LEFT OUT, AND WHY -- this is a judgement,
not a measurement, and it is written down so it can be argued with. Every
one of them is brighter than M 94, which is the fifteenth that stayed:

  NAME CMa Dwarf Galaxy   V -0.1   no dimensions in SIMBAD. A disputed
                                   overdensity inside the Milky Way's own
                                   disc; there is nothing to point at.
  NAME SDG (Sagittarius)  V  3.6   no dimensions. A dwarf spheroidal
                                   behind the galactic centre, some ten
                                   degrees across.
  Z 75-118                V  7.0   0.48 arcmin across at V 7.0. The
                                   magnitude does not fit the size, and a
                                   seventh-magnitude galaxy half an arcminute
                                   wide would be famous. Not credible.
  MCG-06-07-001 (Fornax)  V  7.4   27.5 arcmin. Dwarf spheroidal.
  AM 0311-513             V  7.8   no dimensions.
  NAME Sculptor Dwarf     V  8.6   15.3 arcmin. Dwarf spheroidal.

The dwarf spheroidals are the interesting exclusion. Their INTEGRATED
magnitude is bright because they are enormous, but the light is spread so
thin that no eye and no camera on a tracker sees them as a galaxy -- they
are resolved star fields, found by counting stars, not by looking. An app
that points you at one is lying about what is there. The Magellanic Clouds
are the opposite case and stay: also enormous, also nearby, and plainly
visible to the naked eye from anywhere south enough to see them.

Positions are J2000 and are precessed to the date like every other
catalogue object in the app. Sizes are the major and minor axes in
arcminutes, used to draw each one at its true size on the sky.
